clue.text: Help out when gold potty lost in bathroom?

indicators.note: potty means crazy or daft, so the letters of the words before it are sent mad and rearranged

explanation.surface: A plea for help after a gold toilet seat has vanished somewhere in the bathroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potty' looks like the bathroom object but is the anagram signal working on HELP OUT WHEN GOLD, all fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gone down the plughole is wasted for good, and in a bathroom the plughole is literally where things vanish.

clue.text: Where might one find each, so at least possible?

parts.note: EA is the usual abbreviation for each; read as an instruction, the answer places these two pieces between the first and last letters of a word, rebuilding that word

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about where things belong, concluding they are at least feasible.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as wordplay: EA (the abbreviation for each) and SO sit within the bounds (first and last letters) of R-EA-SO-N.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything within the bounds of reason is reasonable, so at the very least it is a plausible possibility.

clue.text: Small flat dish: slip in fruit

parts.note: a pie is a baked dish

indicators.note: in tells us the word for slip goes inside the fruit

parts.note: a date is the fruit of the date palm
to err is to slip up or make a mistake

explanation.surface: A recipe direction: a little flat plate, with something sliding into the fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small flat dish' wants to be one item; 'Small flat' is the definition and 'dish' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pied-à-terre is a modest second home, usually a compact apartment kept in town for occasional stays.

clue.text: Author taking month to pen a novel that's half-hearted

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the month's letters surround the rest

parts.note: Nov is the short form of November

indicators.note: the word for novel has a double-letter heart, and losing half of it leaves only one of the two middle letters

parts.note: a novel is a book

explanation.surface: A writer spends a month producing a novel that lacks real commitment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' drops one of the two middle letters of the book, and 'to pen' wraps the month round A plus what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Vladimir Nabokov was the Russian-American writer of Lolita and Pale Fire.

clue.text: Short table for fish

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the final letter of the word for table is dropped

parts.note: a chart is a table of data

explanation.surface: Looks like a brief menu or tide chart giving the fish on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' docks the last letter of CHART.
explanation.definitionFit: The char is a freshwater fish of the salmon family, found in cold lakes.

clue.text: What one might say about sweet jar that seems sensible to some people

definitions.text: What one might say about sweet jar that seems sensible to some people

parts.words: What one might say about sweet jar that seems sensible to some people
parts.note: a jar of liquorice allsorts holds every kind of sweet, and the stock saying excuses behaviour that only some find sensible

explanation.surface: A remark about a jar of sweets, and about odd things some people find perfectly reasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: Liquorice Allsorts are a British mixed sweet, so a jar of them literally takes allsorts; the saying means people differ.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb, short for 'it takes all sorts to make a world', tolerates odd tastes and choices.

clue.text: Drop a brick on toe: sit up if not broken

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the letters before it are reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone drops a brick on their toe and is told to sit up unless it is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop a brick' reads as a literal accident, but it is British slang for a tactless blunder; the anagram works on ON TOE SIT UP IF NOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for saying something tactless or embarrassing; dropping a brick is the British version of a gaffe.

clue.text: Country India commended?

indicators.note: the clue word commended splits as com plus mended, and mended means repaired or put back together, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A nation praises India, perhaps in a diplomatic statement.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'commended' as COM + 'mended': INDIA plus COM, rearranged, gives the Caribbean island nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominica is an island republic in the eastern Caribbean, a separate state from the Dominican Republic.

clue.text: Booty I see lying back in bath

indicators.note: lying back means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: booty is slang for the backside, as is butt
oh is what one says on seeing or understanding

explanation.surface: Someone with a nice backside reclines in the bath, and an onlooker notices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booty' suggests treasure but is slang for the bottom; 'lying back' turns the whole charade round.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot tub is a large heated outdoor bathing tub, often bubbling, for soaking in.

clue.text: Hounds gone to the dogs — with bare paws?

indicators.note: gone to the dogs means ruined or fallen apart, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pack of hounds has gone to the dogs, padding about without boots on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone to the dogs' looks like part of a canine picture but is the anagram signal on HOUNDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Unshod means without shoes, as a horse with no shoes is unshod; a dog's paws are bare naturally.

clue.text: See 2
Spare item cut

indicators.note: cut means trimmed short, so the final letter is removed

parts.note: a thing is an item

explanation.surface: A spare item has been cut down, like a superfluous part trimmed off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spare' looks like an adjective describing the item, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare can mean lean or meagre, as in a spare frame, a sense shared with thin.

clue.text: Fifth in Crufts, I'm amazed obedient dog moped, say

indicators.note: fifth in points at the fifth letter of the following word, counting from its start

parts.note: wow is an exclamation of amazement
a heeler is a dog that walks to heel, obediently at its owner's side

explanation.surface: At Crufts, Britain's big dog show, a fifth-placed obedient dog sulks and someone gasps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moped' looks like the past tense of mope, fitting a disappointed dog, but it is the motorbike. Crufts is a famous British dog show.
explanation.definitionFit: A moped is a small motorised bike, one example of a vehicle running on two wheels.

clue.text: Musical compositions, those going over some people's heads?

definitions.text: those going over some people's heads?

parts.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical
pieces are musical compositions

explanation.surface: Musical works that are too sophisticated for some listeners to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical compositions' reads as one phrase, but 'Musical' is the show HAIR and 'going over heads' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairpiece is a toupee or wig, which literally sits over the wearer's head.

clue.text: Put out present in elevated position

indicators.note: out means not in its normal state, so the letters of the word before it are disordered

parts.note: here means present, as in a register

explanation.surface: An instruction to set out a gift on a high shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' looks like a gift but means here, as in answering a register; 'out' scrambles only the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Up there points to a raised place overhead, a high spot above the speaker.

clue.text: African animal, howler gobbling bird with wings pulled off

indicators.note: gobbling means swallowing, so the second piece is taken inside the first

parts.note: a howler is a blunder, a gaffe

indicators.note: the wings of a word are its outer letters, so only the middle of the word bird is kept

explanation.surface: A howler monkey eats a bird after pulling its wings off, near an African animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'howler' suggests the monkey but means a blunder; 'with wings pulled off' strips B and D from BIRD, leaving IR.
explanation.definitionFit: The giraffe is the tall long-necked grazer of the African savanna.

clue.text: Genius running oxygen tunnel into nose

indicators.note: into says the pieces before it go inside the word for nose

parts.note: to nose is to pry
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
to dig is to tunnel

explanation.surface: A brilliant mind is running oxygen through a tube into a patient's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nose' looks like a noun in the medical picture; it is the verb, PRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A prodigy is a person, often young, with exceptional talent, which a genius also has.

clue.text: Material popped up: three books with real worth initially condemned

indicators.note: condemned means doomed or wrecked, so the collected letters are rearranged

parts.note: B is an abbreviation for book, so three books give three Bs

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Something popped up: three books of real value were condemned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'popped up' reads as one verb, but 'Material popped' is the definition and 'up' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Bubble wrap is plastic packing sheet with air pockets, which people famously enjoy bursting.

clue.text: Ladies and gentlemen relaxed briefly

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is removed

parts.note: loose means relaxed or slack

explanation.surface: A compere addresses the audience as ladies and gentlemen, who sit back relaxed for a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ladies and gentlemen' sounds like a form of address; it means public toilets, labelled Ladies and Gentlemen in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Public toilets in Britain are often signed Ladies and Gentlemen, and loo is British slang for toilet.

clue.text: You smooth figure!

parts.note: thou is the old word for you
to sand is to make smooth

explanation.surface: A compliment: you are a smooth operator with a fine figure!
explanation.walkthrough: 'figure' reads as a person's shape, but it is a number.
explanation.definitionFit: A thousand is a number, and figure here means a numeral rather than a body shape.

clue.text: War god somewhat miserable after uprising

indicators.note: uprising, in a down clue, means the letters are read from bottom to top
somewhat means partly, so some letters are taken from inside the next word

explanation.surface: A god of war is rather miserable after a rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat' takes SERA from inside miserable; 'uprising' turns it round. 'uprising' looks like a rebellion fitting a war god.
explanation.definitionFit: Ares is the Greek god of war, counterpart to the Roman Mars.

clue.text: Hot first of all in equatorial region, opposite then is cold

indicators.note: first of all points to the opening letter of every one of the following words

explanation.surface: A weather report: hot in the tropics, but the opposite region is cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' reads as temperature in the weather picture but means sexy.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot is slang for sexually arousing, the same sense as erotic.

clue.text: Swear, finding head of pigeon on shelf

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: a ledge is a narrow shelf

explanation.surface: Someone curses on finding a pigeon's head on the shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swear' suggests cursing; it means to promise.
explanation.definitionFit: To pledge is to promise solemnly, the sense of swearing an oath.

clue.text: Holding swallow tail in fist, pluck bird

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the word for pluck surrounds the other pieces

parts.note: grit means pluck or courage
to swallow is to eat

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Clutching a swallow's tail feathers in one's fist, someone plucks a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallow' and 'pluck' both look like bird words here; they are the verb eat and the noun courage.
explanation.definitionFit: The great tit is a common European songbird with a black head and yellow breast.
